problem: Robot performance is usually measured by post-hoc surveys that interrupt interaction and give coarse feedback. Prior implicit-feedback work covers only stationary lab tasks, not dynamic, crowded robot navigation where human behavior depends on both the robot and the environment.
motivation: Being able to infer a person's perception of a robot's navigation from implicit cues (spatial behavior, gaze, facial expression) would allow scalable, burden-free evaluation and supervision, e.g. detecting mistakes or providing a reward signal. It is unclear which cues matter during navigation, how models compare with human observers, and whether models generalize to new users and to the real world.
key_idea: Collect a VR dataset (SEAN TOGETHER) of people following a guiding robot with in-situ 5-point ratings of competence, surprise and intent clarity, then compare humans and supervised models predicting these ratings from facial vs navigation features, including unseen-user generalization and a real-world demo.
insight: Spatial and navigation features in context (robot-centered poses, goal, occupancy, gaze) carry more information than facial expressions: Nav.-Only and Nav.+Facial beat Facial-Only for both humans and ML. Predicting exact 5-class ratings is hard (average F1 about 0.25 on unseen users), but binary low-vs-not-low performance is far easier (about 0.62), so directionality is what generalizes. ML beats humans by exploiting dominant behavior patterns, while humans do better on mixed behaviors and unusual reactions.
method: SEAN TOGETHER data collection: 60 participants wore a VR headset (Vive Pro Eye) as avatars and followed a simulated Fetch robot in a warehouse (SEAN 2.0) through 4 tasks. The robot switched between Nav-Stack, Spinning and Wrong-Way behaviors, and the sim was paused 4 s before and 8 s after each switch to collect 5-point ratings of competence, surprise and intent clarity.

Feature sets: Facial (73 blend-shape features plus gaze); Nav. (robot-relative poses of the participant and agents within 7.2 m, goal pose, 7.2x7.2 m occupancy crop encoded by ResNet-18, and gaze). Inputs are 8 s windows at 5 Hz (40 timesteps).

Human baseline: 100 Prolific annotators predicted ratings for 120 samples (2 per participant) under Facial-Only, Nav.-Only and Nav.+Facial renderings, 10 annotators per sample; analyzed with linear mixed models.

ML models: Random Forest (100 trees), MLP (5.4M params), message-passing GNN (2.1M), Transformer (6.5M), plus a random baseline. Trained with cross-entropy and Adam/AdamW, with grid-searched hyperparameters. Evaluated on the same 120 samples (2280 train, 569 val).
Generalization test: leave-one-participant-out cross-validation on Nav.+Facial, scored for 5-class and binary labels (1-2 vs 3-5).

Real-world demo: a Pioneer 3-DX robot was followed by 45 pedestrians on campus, yielding 235 Nav.-Only examples. Random Forests were trained on real data or on VR data with a restricted field of view and at most 5 people, and evaluated as VR→VR, VR→Real and Real→Real.

setting.backbone: Random Forest, MLP, GNN and Transformer classifiers (trained from scratch) with ResNet-18 map encoding
setting.model_size: RF with 100 trees; MLP 5.4M, GNN 2.1M, Transformer 6.5M parameters
setting.training_data: SEAN TOGETHER VR dataset: 60 participants, about 2,969 samples (2280 train, 569 val, 120 test); real-world set of 235 examples from 45 pedestrians
setting.observation: Robot-centric poses of the user and pedestrians, goal position, 2D occupancy map crop, gaze, and (VR only) facial blend shapes; real world uses Nav.-Only features from RGB-D people tracking and LiDAR
setting.action_space: none (perception prediction task, not a navigation policy); the robot follows a fixed ROS Navigation Stack with scripted behaviors
setting.simulator: SEAN 2.0 with VR (Unity/ROS) and a real-world Pioneer 3-DX
setting.privileged: In VR, ground-truth poses of all agents and the map are used; the real-world demo uses onboard people tracking and the localization map

numbers_note: Not a navigation benchmark paper. Numbers are prediction F1/accuracy/MAE on the paper's own dataset. The leave-one-out generalization results (average F1 0.25 multiclass, 0.62 binary) are given only in a figure and text.
results: ML models (especially Random Forest) outperformed human annotators and the random baseline in F1 for all three dimensions, e.g. competence F1 0.38 (RF, Nav.+Facial) vs 0.29 (humans). Binary prediction on unseen users roughly doubled F1 (0.62 vs 0.25). Real-world Real→Real binary F1 was 0.61/0.58/0.60, close to the VR numbers.
limitations: Single VR warehouse and two indoor real-world sites; the VR setup, the blend-shape face rendering and the sim-to-real gap may bias behavior and ratings.
5-class prediction is weak, human and ML F1 are low, the dataset is small, and real-world results have high variance (std up to 0.4).
Facial features were not captured in the real world (occlusion); robot behaviors were scripted, and no closed-loop adaptation of robot behavior was tested.
builds_on: Empathic robot implicit feedback (Cui et al.)
